The page asserts that gradients vanish; the same W_h appearing once per timestep is why, and a loop showing the product shrink is what makes that inevitable rather than mysterious.

The placement of the norm relative to the residual is this page's central architectural claim and the two orderings are indistinguishable in prose.

title: Prefill & Decode Phases

title: Query, Key, Value Attention

viz: interactive QKV matrix computation showing attention scores and how each token attends to others — hover token to see its attention pattern
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for scaled dot-product attention with the operations in their load-bearing order: scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k), apply the causal mask as -inf BEFORE the softmax, softmax, then @ V. Follow it with the multi-head reshape (B, T, H, d_head).transpose(1, 2). Masking after the softmax is the classic bug and only code shows the ordering.

title: RWKV Model
description: RWKV: the RNN-Transformer hybrid that achieves linear complexity inference with transformer-quality results. Receptance, Weight, Key, Value formulation and how it differs from standard attention.
viz: comparison chart: RWKV linear recurrence vs transformer O(n²) attention — animated complexity scaling
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the WKV recurrence in its numerically stable running-maximum form, showing the O(1) per-token state update carried forward as (a, b, max) rather than a growing sequence. The page's whole claim is linear-time inference with transformer-quality mixing; the constant-size carried state is the mechanism and it cannot be seen in a diagram.

title: Chinchilla Scaling Law
description: Hoffmann et al. (2022) optimal compute allocation: equal scaling of model size and tokens. Why Chinchilla showed GPT-3 was undertrained, and how it changed model design.
viz: interactive scaling law chart — drag compute budget slider to see optimal model size vs tokens tradeoff

title: LLM Development Bottlenecks
description: The two macro bottlenecks constraining LLM progress: training data (quantity, quality, depletion) and electricity/compute (energy cost, data center capacity, chip availability).
viz: dual bottleneck diagram showing data and energy constraints with current state indicators and projected timelines

title: Post-Training: Why & How
description: Why pretrained models need post-training (factual errors, harmful outputs, instruction-following gaps) and the three main solutions: SFT, preference finetuning (RLHF/DPO), and Best-of-N.
viz: before/after comparison of raw pretrained vs post-trained model outputs with interactive flow through SFT → RLHF → DPO pipeline

title: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
description: Full RLHF pipeline: SFT → reward model training from human preferences → PPO optimization. Key components, reward hacking, and why it's expensive.
viz: animated 3-stage pipeline: SFT model → human raters comparing outputs → reward model → PPO loop with reward signal flowing back
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the PPO objective actually used in RLHF: ratio = exp(logp_new - logp_old), the clipped surrogate min(ratio * A, clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * A), and the explicit KL-to-reference penalty subtracted from the reward. The KL term is what stops the reward hacking the page describes, and it is a line of code, not a paragraph.

title: DPO — Direct Preference Optimization
description: How DPO eliminates the reward model and RL loop by directly optimizing on preference pairs. Mathematical intuition, comparison to RLHF, and when to prefer each.
viz: side-by-side RLHF vs DPO pipeline diagram showing DPO's elimination of reward model and PPO stages
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the DPO loss -logsigmoid(beta * ((logp_w - logp_ref_w) - (logp_l - logp_ref_l))), computed over a preference pair. Seeing the reference log-probabilities cancel into a difference of differences is what makes the page's claim — that the reward model is implicit and the RL loop unnecessary — checkable rather than asserted.

title: Best-of-N / Beam Search
description: Inference-time compute scaling via Best-of-N sampling and beam search. How generating multiple candidates and scoring with a reward model improves output quality without retraining.
viz: animated tree of N generated sequences with scoring and selection — beam search pruning animation

title: Fine-Tuning: When, Why & Decision Framework
description: When to fine-tune vs prompt-engineer vs RAG, the two capabilities it improves (domain knowledge, instruction following), cost realities, and the decision tree for choosing your approach.
viz: interactive decision tree: start with your use case → click through conditions → arrive at recommended approach (prompt / RAG / finetune)

title: Fine-Tuning Types: Full, Partial, PEFT
description: Full fine-tuning vs partial (frozen layers) vs Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT). LoRA, adapter-based, and soft prompt methods — tradeoffs in memory, data needs, and serving.
viz: model layer diagram showing which layers are frozen/trainable in each method — toggle between full / partial / LoRA modes

title: LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation
description: LoRA's core idea: freeze original weights, train low-rank decomposition matrices A and B. Rank selection, alpha scaling, how adapters are merged at inference, and QLoRA.
viz: animated weight matrix decomposition: W → W₀ + AB where A and B are low-rank — interactive rank slider showing parameter count reduction
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the LoRA forward W0 @ x + (alpha / r) * B @ (A @ x) with A gaussian-initialised and B initialised to zeros, plus the merge step W = W0 + (alpha / r) * B @ A. The zero-init of B is why training begins exactly at the base model's behaviour, and the alpha/r factor is why changing rank does not silently rescale the update.

title: Model Distillation
description: Knowledge distillation: training a small student model to mimic a large teacher model using soft labels and intermediate representations. The distillation data pipeline path.
viz: animated teacher → soft logits → student training loop with temperature-scaled probability distribution comparison
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the distillation loss: KL(softmax(student/T) || softmax(teacher/T)) multiplied by T^2, added to alpha * cross_entropy(student, hard_labels). The T^2 rescaling is dropped in most implementations and silently shrinks the soft-label gradient as temperature rises — exactly the sort of detail this page exists to teach.

title: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning & Model Merging
description: Simultaneous vs sequential fine-tuning, catastrophic forgetting, and model merging techniques (weight summing, layer stacking, concatenation).
viz: sequential finetuning showing catastrophic forgetting on task A when training task B — vs model merging combining both
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for task arithmetic: build each task vector tau_i = theta_finetuned_i - theta_base, then merge as theta_base + sum(lambda_i * tau_i), followed by the TIES sign-election step that drops parameters whose task vectors disagree in sign. The page names model merging; the subtraction-and-sum is the entire operation and is three lines.

title: Fine-Tuning Hyperparameters
description: Learning rate, batch size, epochs, and prompt loss weight — what each controls, typical ranges, and how to tune them systematically.
viz: interactive learning rate vs loss curve — drag sliders for LR, batch size, epochs and watch training curve change
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block computing effective batch size as per_device_batch * grad_accum_steps * world_size next to a linear-warmup-then-cosine learning-rate schedule evaluated over the first few hundred steps. The page lists the knobs separately; the code shows they are coupled — doubling grad accumulation changes the effective batch and therefore the learning rate you should have picked.

title: Memory Bottlenecks in Fine-Tuning
description: Why fine-tuning needs more memory than inference: forward + backward pass, optimizer states, gradient checkpointing, numerical precision, and quantization.
viz: GPU memory breakdown bar chart for inference vs full fine-tuning vs LoRA — showing model weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block that adds up fine-tuning memory for a concrete parameter count: weights (2 bytes in bf16) + gradients (2) + Adam states (4 for m, 4 for v, and 4 for the fp32 master copy) = 16 bytes per parameter, then activations as a separate term, and what gradient checkpointing removes from that second term. The page argues fine-tuning needs far more memory than inference; the per-parameter arithmetic is the proof.

title: Token Sampling: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P
description: How LLMs select the next token: temperature scaling, top-K filtering, nucleus (top-P) sampling — their effects on diversity vs coherence.
viz: interactive probability distribution over vocabulary — drag temperature / top-K / top-P sliders and watch distribution reshape in real-time
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block applying the sampling pipeline in order — divide logits by temperature, apply the top-k cutoff, apply the top-p nucleus cutoff on the sorted cumulative distribution, softmax, then draw. Order is the point: applying top-p before temperature, or renormalising twice, changes the distribution, and only a listing pins the sequence down.

title: LLM Evaluation Metrics
description: Exact match, lexical similarity (edit distance, ROUGE, BLEU), semantic similarity (cosine), LLM-as-judge, and their biases (self, position, verbosity).
viz: side-by-side metric comparison: enter two texts and see all metric scores computed live with explanation of what each captures
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block computing ROUGE-L from the longest common subsequence and BLEU from modified n-gram precision with its brevity penalty, on the same candidate/reference pair, printing both scores. The page's argument is that lexical metrics disagree with each other and with meaning; two numbers from one pair of sentences demonstrates it in a way a table of definitions cannot.

title: Evaluation Pipeline Design

viz: evaluation pipeline flow diagram — click each stage to see what can go wrong and how to detect it

title: Loss Functions: Cross-Entropy & Perplexity

viz: animated probability distribution with live cross-entropy and perplexity computation as predicted distribution shifts toward/away from true distribution

The shift is the implementation detail that silently produces a plausible-looking but wrong loss curve when omitted, and it is invisible in the formula the page currently gives.

title: Model Evaluation Workflow

title: Prompt Attacks & Defenses
description: Prompt injection, jailbreaking, prompt extraction, information extraction — attack vectors and defense strategies with violation rate and false refusal rate metrics.
viz: attack/defense game: animated prompt injection attempt flowing through defense layers — see which layers catch what

title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description: Full RAG pipeline: indexing → querying → retrieval → generation. Term-based vs embedding-based vs hybrid retrieval, chunking, query rewriting, and reranking.
viz: animated end-to-end RAG pipeline — query enters, flows through retriever, top-K chunks surface, generator produces grounded answer
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the hybrid retrieval the page describes: Okapi BM25 with its idf = ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5)) and the k1/b term-saturation factor, cosine similarity over embeddings, then Reciprocal Rank Fusion combining the two rankings as sum of 1/(k + rank) with k = 60. Fusion on ranks rather than on scores is why the two retrievers can be combined at all without calibrating them.

title: Vector Search & KNN
description: Embedding-based retrieval, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms (HNSW, IVF, FAISS), exact vs approximate tradeoffs, and two-stage retrieval (cheap retriever + KNN rerank).
viz: interactive 2D vector space — plot query point, see K nearest neighbors highlighted, toggle between exact vs approximate search

The page is careful that O(log N) is expected rather than guaranteed; the beam width appearing as a tunable in the code is where that recall/latency trade actually lives.

title: AI Agents: Observe → Decide → Act → Learn
description: Agent loop, tool types (knowledge augmentation, capability extension, write actions), planning vs execution separation, observability, and failure modes.
viz: animated agent loop diagram — observe env → plan → select tool → execute → observe result — with failure injection points highlighted

The page's loop must be one loop and not two; a single listing pins the contract, and the step budget is the difference between an agent and a runaway.

title: Agent Memory Systems

viz: agent with context window filling up → overflow into long-term memory store → retrieval on next turn — animated capacity and retrieval flow

viz: data quality radar chart — adjust 6 quality dimensions (relevance, consistency, format, uniqueness, compliance, coverage) and see impact score

viz: inference optimization decision tree — select your bottleneck type → see ranked optimization techniques with expected speedup indicators

title: Speculative Decoding
description: How a small draft model generates candidate tokens that the large target model verifies in parallel — achieving 2-3x speedup without quality loss.
viz: animated draft model generating K tokens → target model verifying all in parallel → accepted/rejected tokens highlighted
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the accept/reject step: accept the draft token when u <= p_target(x) / p_draft(x), and on rejection resample from the normalised residual max(0, p_target - p_draft). That renormalised residual is what makes speculative decoding distribution-preserving rather than merely fast, and it is the part almost every summary of the technique omits.

title: Model & Tensor Parallelism
description: Tensor parallelism (split layers across GPUs), pipeline parallelism (split layers sequentially), context parallelism, sequence parallelism — when and why each.
viz: multi-GPU diagram showing how model layers are split across devices in tensor vs pipeline parallelism modes — toggle between strategies

title: Agent Observability
description: Tracing, monitoring, and debugging multi-step agent runs — the three pillars of observability (traces, metrics, evaluation), what to instrument, and the tools that matter in production.
viz: interactive agent trace viewer with 12-step simulated run — click spans to inspect details, animated replay, cost tracking bar, color-coded span types

title: Production LLM Serving
description: The decode bottleneck and the three pillars that solve it — PagedAttention, continuous batching, and Flash Attention — converging in vLLM, TGI, and TensorRT-LLM into a unified serving stack.
viz: interactive serving timeline showing continuous batching in action — requests arriving, finishing mid-batch, new ones inserted at each decode step, with live GPU utilization gauge

title: Quantization for Inference
description: int8, int4, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF, NF4 — how post-training quantization reduces model size 2-4x with minimal quality loss, and how to choose the right scheme for your deployment.
viz: interactive quantization explorer — select a precision level (fp16, int8, int4, NF4) and see the VRAM footprint change for Llama 3 70B, with per-layer quality degradation estimates
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block contrasting the two weight-only methods this page distinguishes: AWQ searching a per-output-channel scale s that minimises error on the activation-salient channels before rounding, against GPTQ's Hessian-guided column-by-column OBQ update that compensates the not-yet-quantised weights after each step. Both are W4A16 and they are easy to blur together in prose; their inner loops are not alike.

title: KV Cache Management
description: How the Key-Value cache grows during autoregressive decoding, why it becomes the memory bottleneck at long context, and how PagedAttention, GQA/MQA, and prefix caching manage it.
viz: animated KV cache filling up token-by-token with visual memory blocks — toggle between naive contiguous allocation (fragmentation) and PagedAttention (packed pages, zero waste)
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block computing KV cache bytes as 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * dtype_bytes for a concrete model, showing the GQA divisor shrinking n_kv_heads relative to n_query_heads, and the block-table indirection PagedAttention uses to allocate that in fixed blocks. The page says the cache becomes the bottleneck; the formula says at which sequence length.

title: Flash Attention
description: How tiled attention keeps computation in SRAM to avoid materializing the full N×N attention matrix in HBM — 2-4x speedup, O(N) memory, mathematically identical output to standard attention.
viz: animated side-by-side comparison of standard attention (full N×N matrix in HBM with O(N²) memory) vs Flash Attention (tiled blocks computed in SRAM with O(N) memory) — toggle sequence length
gaps: Add a worked <pre> code block for the online-softmax rescaling across tiles: carry the running max m and running denominator l, and on each new tile update m_new = max(m, m_tile) and l = l * exp(m - m_new) + l_tile * exp(m_tile - m_new), rescaling the accumulated output by the same factor. That correction is the whole reason attention can be tiled without materialising the N x N matrix, and prose cannot convey it.

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
description: The open protocol that standardises how LLM applications connect to external tools and data, replacing N×M bespoke integrations with one client/server contract — the host/client/server split, what a server exposes, and why a shared protocol changes agent architecture.
viz: interactive N×M-to-N+M integration explorer — drag app and data-source counts on two sliders and watch the connector graph redraw, bespoke-integration edge count exploding as N×M while the MCP-mediated count grows as N+M; click any server node to expand its exposed capability list and trace one tool call end-to-end through host → client → server → result

title: GRPO & RL with Verifiable Rewards
description: Group Relative Policy Optimization drops PPO's critic network and estimates the advantage baseline from the mean reward of a group of sampled completions — the algorithm behind modern reasoning models, paired with verifiable rewards from executable checks rather than a learned preference model.
viz: side-by-side PPO vs GRPO training-step animation — PPO shows the extra critic network and its memory footprint, GRPO samples a group of G completions for one prompt and computes each advantage as (reward − group mean) / group std, with a live histogram of the group's rewards and a toggle to switch the reward source between a learned preference model and a verifiable checker (unit test passes / answer matches) to show how the signal changes

title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
description: Replacing the dense FFN with many expert FFNs and a router that activates only top-k per token — decoupling total parameters from per-token compute, plus the load-balancing problem that makes or breaks training, shared experts, and why expert parallelism dominates MoE serving cost.
viz: interactive MoE layer where you type a sentence and watch each token get routed — router logits shown as a bar chart per token, top-k experts highlighted, and a live expert-utilisation heatmap that develops hot and dead experts as you feed more tokens; toggle the load-balancing loss on and off to watch routing collapse onto a few experts, and a slider for total-vs-active parameters showing the FLOPs saved against the VRAM still required

title: Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute
description: Spending more compute at inference instead of training — long chain-of-thought, sampling-and-selection, and effort/budget controls — how the accuracy-vs-inference-compute curve behaves, and where spending more thinking tokens stops paying for itself.
viz: log-scale accuracy-vs-test-time-compute curve you can explore by dragging a thinking-budget slider — the sampled reasoning traces appear as branching paths that get longer and more numerous as budget rises, with a cost meter ticking up in tokens and the curve visibly flattening past the knee; toggle between strategies (single long CoT, best-of-N, self-consistency majority vote) to compare their curves on the same axes

title: Structured Output & Constrained Decoding
description: How schema enforcement actually works at the token level: compile the schema or grammar to an automaton, and at each step mask the logits of every token that cannot legally continue the parse. Covers JSON mode vs strict schema vs full grammar constraints, the token-boundary problem, and why valid output is not correct output.
viz: token-by-token constrained decoding walkthrough — paste a JSON schema, watch it compile into a state machine, then step through generation seeing the full vocabulary distribution beside the masked one, with disallowed tokens greyed out and the current parser state highlighted; a toggle for unconstrained vs constrained shows the model's original top-token being suppressed, illustrating the distribution-distortion tradeoff

title: Multimodal Models & VLMs
description: How vision-language models turn pixels into tokens the LLM can attend to — the vision encoder plus projector pattern, native early-fusion alternatives, image tiling and resolution handling, and why image tokens dominate the context budget in document-heavy workloads.
viz: upload or pick an image and watch it flow through the pipeline — patchification grid overlaid on the image, each patch becoming an embedding, the projector mapping them into the LLM's token space, and a running counter showing how many text-token-equivalents the image consumed; a resolution slider shows the tile count and token cost climbing quadratically, and a toggle contrasts encoder-plus-projector against native early fusion

title: Long-Context Techniques
description: How context windows grew from thousands to millions of tokens: RoPE and its scaling variants (position interpolation, NTK-aware, YaRN), ALiBi, and sparse or compressed attention — plus why a bigger window does not fix mid-context recall, prefill latency, or KV-cache memory.
viz: RoPE rotation explorer — a unit circle showing query/key vectors rotating by position, with a slider that extends sequence length past the training window so you can watch the rotations alias and attention scores degrade; then apply position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN and see the frequency bands rescale and the degradation flatten, alongside a needle-in-a-haystack retrieval heatmap (position × context length) that stays stubbornly weak in the middle no matter how far the window is extended

title: Prompt Caching Mechanics
description: Caching the prefill KV state of a stable prompt prefix so repeat requests skip recomputation — exact-prefix matching semantics, why any byte change invalidates everything after it, cache-write vs cache-read pricing, TTLs, and how to order a prompt so the cache actually hits.
viz: prompt-prefix cache simulator — compose a prompt from draggable blocks (system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, user turn) and reorder them, with a live cache-hit meter showing how much of the prefix is reused across a simulated request stream; drop a timestamp or request ID into an early block and watch the hit rate collapse to zero, with a running cost readout splitting cache-write, cache-read and uncached input tokens

title: Model Routing & Cost Cascades
description: Sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it — routers that classify difficulty up front versus cascades that escalate on a confidence or verification signal, how to calibrate the threshold on a golden set, and why the narrowing price gap between tiers changed the economics.
viz: interactive routing simulator over a stream of 1,000 mixed-difficulty queries — drag the escalation threshold and watch queries flow through the small tier or spill to the frontier tier in real time, with live blended cost, accuracy, and p95 latency updating together; a Pareto plot traces the cost-quality frontier as you sweep the threshold, and a toggle switches between up-front routing and cascade-with-verification so you can compare their curves

title: Agent Evaluation Methodology
description: Evaluating multi-step agents where the final answer hides the process — outcome versus trajectory evaluation, programmatic checks against LLM-as-judge and its known biases, per-step attribution of failures, and building a regression suite that survives non-determinism.
viz: agent trajectory inspector over a batch of simulated runs — a grid of traces coloured by outcome, click one to expand its step-by-step tool calls and see where the run diverged from the reference trajectory; a failure-attribution bar chart splits failures by cause (wrong tool, bad arguments, hallucinated result, gave up early, loop), and a slider that adds run-to-run noise shows how many repeat runs you need before the pass-rate confidence interval is tight enough to gate a deploy
